title: Does Deterministic Generate–Validate–Repair Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Confirmatory Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired confirmatory study (n = 200 intent→configuration tasks) to test whether a deterministic generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator reduces validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline. The run used a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation semantics and a primary deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution consumed 200 model calls (one shared initial generation per task); no repair calls were issued because every initial candidate passed the validator. Paired contingency: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; estimate of paired difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Because the baseline validator‑detected unsafe incidence was 0% on this task bank, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be meaningfully evaluated. We present the sealed design, execution accounting, representative examples, the preregistered contamination holdout evidence (Mininet 10% holdout → 20 tasks; analysis/contamination_summary.csv records zero disagreements), and an artifact‑grounded discussion of operational implications and threats to validity (preregistration id: cnsms2026-gvr-effectiveness-02).

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→configuration translation with generative language models promises operational productivity gains but risks incorrect or unsafe changes that can cause outages, policy violations, or degraded service. Prior proposals therefore integrate LLM generation with deterministic validators and repair loops (generate–validate–repair, GVR) so that unsafe candidates can be detected and corrected before application. The operational value of automated repair depends on (i) the baseline prevalence of validator‑detectable failures produced by the chosen generator/prompting policy; (ii) the validator’s coverage and fidelity; and (iii) the repair budget and repair‑prompt effectiveness. We asked a narrowly scoped, preregistered confirmatory question: Does a deterministic GVR pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator materially reduce the incidence of validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only pipeline on a curated 200‑task intent→configuration bank?

Contributions. (1) A sealed preregistered paired design (n = 200) that enforces shared‑initial generation semantics to isolate the effect of applying a deterministic validator+repair to the same generated candidate. (2) A fully archived autonomous execution with deterministic reconciliation and concrete accounting (completed pairs = 200, model_calls_used = 200, repair_calls = 0). (3) An artifact‑grounded null/degenerate confirmatory outcome and interpretation that clarifies when automated repair can and cannot reduce validator‑detected failures, together with reproducibility notes and operational recommendations grounded in the archived artifacts.
sections.related_work: LLMs produce factual errors and are sensitive to prompt formulation and context; mitigation approaches include retrieval grounding, verifier‑assisted repair, bounded/guarded agent architectures, and multi‑step repair workflows [https://openalex.org/W4399803256; https://openalex.org/W4410125989]. Prototype NetOps systems show intent→configuration synthesis feasibility but lack comprehensive, instrumented failure‑rate studies [https://openalex.org/W4399629579; https://openalex.org/W4403635865]. Red‑team audits and configuration‑brittleness analyses highlight that tool descriptions and cross‑tool ambiguity can materially alter agent safety outcomes [10.21203/rs.3.rs-10646209/v1; 10.2139/ssrn.7203631]. Our experiment positions itself among generator→validator→repair proposals by isolating the marginal effect of adding a deterministic repair step for a fixed model and deterministic prompt policy under rigorous preregistration.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and inferential plan. The study preregistration (cnsms2026-gvr-effectiveness-02) fixed a paired design (n = 200 tasks), a single confirmatory test (exact McNemar two‑sided, α = 0.05), and an adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation policy (one initial candidate produced per task and reused for both baseline and guarded conditions). The primary estimand was paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline, reported as absolute and relative reductions; the primary test was exact McNemar and 95% CIs used a bootstrap percentile method (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Power planning assumed baseline unsafe incidence ≈30% and targeted a 50% relative reduction; sample size n = 200 was selected to provide approximate 0.8 power under that assumption.

Task bank and validators. The task bank comprised 200 machine‑checkable intent→configuration problems divided into four topology clusters (enterprise, campus, datacenter, edge; 50 tasks each). Each task encodes an initial state, required final state, workflow constraints (examples: make_before_break, must_be_down_for_fields), and an explicit required_sequence. The primary deterministic checker (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) enforces these constraints and emits structured diagnostics (valid flag, violation codes, parsed_command_count, required_command_count). A Mininet‑based data‑plane emulator was preregistered as a secondary disagreement detector and applied to a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks) to detect validator–emulator mismatches; the contamination artifact analysis/contamination_summary.csv reports zero disagreements for that holdout.

Adapter, model, and generation semantics. The experiment used the hosted model declared in the preregistration (gpt‑5‑mini) invoked via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter. Crucially, the adapter enforced shared_initial generation semantics: for each task the system produced a single initial candidate (deterministic sampling policy) which was reused for both baseline (LLM‑only) and guarded (GVR) conditions. This isolates the effect of applying validation+repair to the same generator output and prevents per‑condition sampling variance from confounding the paired comparison. Adapter accounting in the execution manifest records hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 200}, confirming one shared generation per task.

Repair policy, budgets, and contamination handling. The preregistered repair policy permitted at most one automated repair prompt per task when the primary validator reported violations; up to 200 repair calls were therefore allowed but only if initial candidates failed validation. The contamination_plan deterministically excluded tasks where primary validator vs emulator disagreed from the primary analysis; preregistered sensitivity analyses cover alternate treatments of flagged tasks. Missingness and exclusion rules were fixed in the preregistration and applied deterministically during execution.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and descriptive outcome. The autonomous run completed all planned episodes: completed_episode_count = 400 (shared initial generation reused across conditions) and complete_pair_count = 200. Model_calls_used = 200 (one shared initial generation per task); no repair calls were issued. Condition summaries (analysis/condition_summary.csv) show baseline successes = 200/200 and guarded successes = 200/200 (success_rate = 1.0 for both). The paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0.

Primary inferential result. With zero discordant pairs the observed paired difference estimate = 0.0. The exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. The bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729) is [0.0, 0.0]. Under the preregistered estimand and test the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis is logically untestable on this sample because there were no baseline validator failures for GVR to reduce.

Repair activity and contamination checks. Because no initial candidate failed deterministic_netops_validator_v5, the GVR pipeline applied zero repair prompts and incurred zero repair‑call cost. The preregistered Mininet holdout (10% → 20 tasks) executed as recorded; the analysis artifact analysis/contamination_summary.csv reports no validator–emulator disagreements. Deterministic reconciliation artifacts report all consistency checks passed (pair_accounting_consistent = true; episode_accounting_consistent = true). Provider call accounting shows hosted_model_call_event_count = 200, cache_miss_count = 200, cache_hit_count = 0, reflecting the shared_initial generation design that produced one invocation per task deterministically reused across conditions.

Representative examples and diagnostics. Representative task artifacts (pair‑000001 through pair‑000006) show shared initial generator outputs that matched the task required_sequence and passed validation: validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true and violation_count = 0 in each example record. Difficulty annotations (e.g., make_before_break_uplink_switchover, paired_link_atomic_mtu_change) and parsed_command_count/required_command_count recorded in validator traces verify that tasks exercised medium‑to‑very_hard workflow constraints despite resulting in validator‑satisfying candidates.

Planned but uninvoked analyses. The preregistration included sensitivity analyses for contamination flags and alternative missingness handling and secondary estimands (average repair iterations, GVR‑introduced failure rate, model‑call cost per successful repair). Because no repair attempts and no contamination flags occurred, those preregistered branches produced empty secondary_results (analysis artifacts record these as empty).
sections.discussion:
Conditional interpretation. The degenerate confirmatory outcome demonstrates a practical point: when a fixed generator+prompt policy produces validator‑passing candidates for every item in a workload, a validator‑coupled repair step cannot reduce validator‑detected failures. This is logically tautological but operationally important: the marginal benefit of GVR is conditional on baseline validator failure prevalence and on validator coverage.

Why baseline failures were zero (artifact‑grounded hypotheses). The archived artifacts support several concrete, non‑speculative reasons: (1) the prompt templates and deterministic sampling policy produced candidates that directly encoded task required_sequences (see representative responses in execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt, etc.); (2) the curated task bank encodes explicit workflow constraints that map closely to the validator checks, making correct generation more likely under a constrained prompt policy; (3) the primary validator enforces encoded intent constraints but may omit device‑level or vendor idiosyncratic behaviors detectable only by full end‑to‑end execution; and (4) the shared_initial design precluded per‑condition re‑sampling as an avenue for producing alternate repairable candidates.

Operational recommendations. Practitioners should (a) measure baseline validator failure prevalence on representative workloads before investing heavily in automated repair; (b) prioritize extending validator fidelity (richer device semantics, vendor idiosyncrasies) and end‑to‑end emulation if validator failures are rare; (c) consider multi‑sample or multi‑model generation policies and expanded repair budgets when baseline failures are nontrivial; and (d) include randomized emulator holdouts (as we preregistered) to detect validator blind spots. The archived Mininet holdout evidence (analysis/contamination_summary.csv) confirmed zero disagreements in this run but also revealed a reproducibility gap (missing explicit labeled seed for holdout selection) that practitioners should avoid: always record labeled random seeds for any randomized holdout used in contamination detection.

Threats to validity. Internal validity: preregistration and adapter enforcement protected against post‑hoc changes; however, shared_initial semantics sacrifice external generality by removing per‑condition sampling variance. Construct validity: the deterministic validator checks task‑encoded constraints but may miss emergent device behaviors only visible under full data‑plane emulation or production hardware. External validity: the run used a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini), deterministic sampling, and a curated task bank; results may differ under other models, sampling temperatures, multi‑sample generation, adversarial distributions, or larger repair budgets. Conclusion validity: the McNemar test is uninformative when discordant pairs are zero; nonetheless reporting the observed zero‑discordance outcome is scientifically meaningful and should inform future workload selection and power planning.

Reproducibility and artifact guidance. All key execution artifacts (model‑call logs, validator traces, paired contingency tables, bootstrap parameters, and provider accounting) are archived and referenced in the analysis bundle. The specific contamination artifact analysis/contamination_summary.csv documents the Mininet holdout outcome (20 tasks) and zero disagreements. One reproducibility gap exists: the explicit randomized seed used to select the Mininet holdout is not present as a labeled artifact in the archived bundle; we disclose this gap and recommend that future runs store labeled holdout seeds alongside contamination summaries.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and ran a sealed paired study comparing LLM‑only generation to a deterministic GVR pipeline on 200 NetOps intent→configuration tasks using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Both pipelines produced validator‑passing configurations for every task (n11 = 200; no discordant pairs). The preregistered hypothesis of a ≥50% relative reduction in validator‑detected unsafe changes was therefore not testable on this task bank. The empirical lesson is operational: GVR reduces validator‑detected failures only when such failures exist to be corrected and when validator coverage aligns with realistic device semantics. Future work should measure GVR value on workloads with nontrivial baseline failure prevalence, increase validator fidelity with emulator or device checks, explore multi‑sample/multi‑model generation and larger repair budgets, and ensure labeled randomized seeds for contamination checks to support exact reproducibility. All execution artifacts, logs, and analysis outputs are archived for independent inspection.

disclosure_statement: Disclosure (mandatory). This study executed under the autonomous post‑lock preregistration cnsms2026-gvr-effectiveness-02 and used the hosted model declared as gpt‑5‑mini (provider label: openai_responses) invoked via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family. The exact initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Topic constraints: the human Research Director limited the study to Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps focusing on safety/reliability of generated network changes. Frameworks and tools: code and experiment orchestration used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 framework and the deterministic task generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5). The primary deterministic validator was deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (intent/constraint checks). A Mininet‑based emulator served as the preregistered secondary disagreement detector applied to a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks); the contamination artifact analysis/contamination_summary.csv records zero disagreements. Preregistration and freeze: the experimental plan (estimand, sample size n = 200, paired design, stopping rules, max model calls = 400, repair call budget = 1 per task, shared‑initial generation semantics) was frozen before any model calls. Autonomous execution and artifacts: the run executed autonomously under the frozen plan; model calls, prompts, seeds, validator traces, emulator traces, logs, and the artifact manifest are archived in the execution bundle. Model‑call budget and usage: 200 model calls were used (one shared initial generation per task); up to 200 repair calls were allowed but none were applied because initial candidates passed the validator. Human involvement: the human Research Director selected the topic family and pre‑lock constraints; no human manual editing or selective rewriting of technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock. Deviations and restarts: no post‑preregistration design changes or technical restarts occurred. Known reproducibility gap: the explicit randomized holdout selection seed used for the Mininet contamination check is not present as a labeled artifact in the archived bundle; this absence prevents deterministic reconstruction of the exact holdout selection despite the contamination summary reporting no disagreements. The master prompt archive reference above is the immutable prompt required by the track.
limitations: Task‑bank scope: the confirmatory sample used a curated synthetic/public intent→configuration bank (n = 200); results therefore reflect this bank and may not generalize to broader production workloads or adversarial distributions.

Single‑model and shared‑initial setting: only gpt‑5‑mini (hosted) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation was tested (execution artifacts record hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts shared_initial_generation = 200). Outcomes may differ across model families, independent per‑condition sampling, nonzero temperature sampling, or larger repair budgets.

Validator coverage and oracle limitations: the primary deterministic validator enforces a defined set of syntax/intent constraints; validators can fail to capture real device idiosyncrasies, vendor‑specific behaviors, or emergent failure modes detectable only by end‑to‑end deployment.

Adversarial robustness untested: this confirmatory run did not include active adversarial injection or red‑team tool‑description attacks; prior audits indicate such vectors can bypass naive defenses and remain a separate concern.

Reproducibility gap for contamination check: the randomized holdout selection seed for the Mininet contamination check is absent from the labeled artifacts, preventing exact reconstruction of the holdout selection.

Single repair budget: the GVR pipeline allowed at most one automated repair prompt per task; multi‑step repair strategies, different repair budgets, or human‑in‑the‑loop approvals were not exercised here.
